title: Continuatio Fragmentorum ex Adversariis mathematicis depromptorum

deep.reconstruction:
Context: fragment no. 110, 'Specimen methodi facilis Analysin infinitorum indeterminatam tractandi'. From §5 on it is marked '(Lexell.)' on the previous page, so the ideas may be Lexell's or worked out jointly with Euler. §§1–4 (previous page) produced all algebraic rectifiable plane curves, using x = s cosφ + p, y = s sinφ + q with tanφ = −dp/dq.

This page, §5. New problem: find an algebraic curve whose arc length reduces to a prescribed quadrature ∫P dp.
- Write the curve as the envelope of its tangents. Put dy = n dx, y = n x + p(n) and s = x√(1+n²) + q(n).
- Requiring dy = n dx and ds = √(1+n²) dx gives x dn + dp = 0 and n x dn/√(1+n²) + dq = 0.
- Hence x = −dp/dn, √(1+n²)/n = dp/dq, n = dq/√(dp²−dq²) and √(1+n²) = dp/√(dp²−dq²).
- So y = (p dn − n dp)/dn and s = −dp√(1+n²)/dn + q.
- This is the Legendre-transform (tangential, Clairaut-type) description of a plane curve, with q playing the role of a 'tangential arc function'.

§6. Take q = ∫P dp with P algebraic. Then dq/dp = P is algebraic, so n = P/√(1−P²) and √(1+n²) = 1/√(1−P²). This yields the algebraic curve
- x = −(1−P²)^{3/2} dp/dP,
- y = p − P(1−P²) dp/dP,
- with arc length s = −(1−P²) dp/dP + ∫P dp.
The arc is therefore 'an algebraic quantity plus the given quadrature'.

§§7–8. Generalisations.
- q = T(p) + ∫P dp with T algebraic.
- Then q = T + ∫V(ν) dν, where ν is an algebraic function of p and V an algebraic function of ν such that ∫V dν is the prescribed quadrature.

§§9–10. Extra requirement: the curve is non-rectifiable in general, yet any desired number of its arcs are absolutely (algebraically) rectifiable.
- Write Π:z = ∫₀^z Z dz, with Π:0 = 0.
- Choose ν = (p−α)(p−β)(p−γ)…·(algebraic factor). Then the transcendental part Π(ν(p)) vanishes at p = α, β, γ, ….
- Hence the arc between any two of these parameter values equals the difference of the algebraic parts, i.e. it is algebraic.

Final paragraph: begins the 'main problem', the spherical analogue. Find curves on the sphere with dx² sin²y + dy² = dr², where x is longitude, y is the polar distance and r is arc length, such that their sines and cosines are algebraic.
- Euler sets dx sin y = dr sin ω and dy = dr cos ω, with ω the course angle.
- He multiplies the second relation by sin y, so that its integral −cos y is algebraic.
- He sets cos ω sin y = p cos r + q sin r. This is the spherical counterpart of the plane envelope ansatz; it continues on the next page with cos y = q cos r − p sin r and tan r = dq/dp.

Checked: all plane formulas on this page are correct.
errors: §10 says 'tantum capiatur Z=(p−α)(p−β)(p−γ)', but in the scheme it is ν (the argument z of Π), not the integrand Z, that must vanish at those points. The next sentence indeed uses ν. This is a slip of notation.
§10: 'casibus p−α, p−β, p−γ' should read p=α, p=β, p=γ.
In 'ν = (p−α)(p−β)(p−γ) etc. P' the letter P is reused for an arbitrary algebraic factor, clashing with the integrand P of §6.
§§9–10 do not make explicit that only arcs between two zeros of Π(ν(p)) are algebraic, not arcs from an arbitrary origin. Nor do they note that real curves need |P|<1 (|dq/dp|<1).
§§7–8 do not check that ν must be non-constant and that the zeros of ν must lie on the real branch used.

ideas.what: Representing a plane curve as the envelope of lines y = n x + p(n), with arc length s = x√(1+n²) + q(n), and deriving x, y, s from p and q
ideas.modern_name: Legendre transform / tangential (Clairaut-equation) parametrisation of plane curves
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler and Legendre (Legendre transform, 1787); envelope methods to Leibniz and Clairaut
ideas.where_published: Euler used similar indirect methods for algebraic rectifiable curves in several memoirs on rectifiable curves; exact E-number unsure

ideas.what: Algebraic curve whose arc length equals an algebraic part plus an arbitrary prescribed quadrature ∫P dp
ideas.modern_name: Realising any abelian integral as arc length of an algebraic curve (modulo algebraic terms)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (rectification problems); later Serret and Liouville for elliptic-arc curves
ideas.where_published: Possibly in Euler's papers on curves rectifiable by a given quadrature; unsure

ideas.what: Making the transcendental part Π(ν(p)) vanish at prescribed parameter values by taking ν with prescribed zeros, so the curve has any number of algebraically rectifiable arcs
ideas.modern_name: Construction of non-rectifiable algebraic curves with prescribed rectifiable arcs
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (theme linked to Fagnano's rectifiable differences of elliptic and lemniscatic arcs)

ideas.what: Spherical analogue: curves on the sphere with dx² sin²y + dy² = dr² and algebraic trigonometric data, via cos ω sin y = p cos r + q sin r
ideas.modern_name: Algebraic rectifiable spherical curves / spherical support-function method
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (late papers on rectifiable curves on the sphere)
ideas.where_published: Euler's late memoirs on algebraic rectifiable curves on the sphere (Nova Acta / Opera postuma); exact E-numbers unsure

missed.claim: A clean explicit formula: for any algebraic P(p), the curve x = −(1−P²)^{3/2}/P′ and y = p − P(1−P²)/P′ is algebraic with arc length −(1−P²)/P′ + ∫P dp. Augmented with ν having prescribed zeros, this gives algebraic curves of 'transcendental' length that have any prescribed number of algebraic arcs. This explicit recipe (likely Lexell's write-up) is rarely cited in histories of rectification.
missed.quote: ut non obstante, quod curva non sit rectificabilis, tamen unum, vel duos, vel tres, vel quotcunque volueris habeat arcus absolute rectificabiles
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Mostly historical: an early, fully explicit general construction realising a given quadrature as arc length of an algebraic curve. It is relevant to the history of the Fagnano–Euler–Serret line on curves with rectifiable arcs.

deep.surprise_reason: Correct, elegant but fairly standard Euler/Lexell technique (tangential parametrisation). The general realisation of a quadrature as arc length, and the prescribed-rectifiable-arcs trick, are natural extensions within Euler's known programme on rectifiable curves. It is partly attributable to Lexell and likely echoed in published memoirs.
transcription_corrections: In §10 the image prints 'casibus p−α, p−β, p−γ'; the intended meaning is p=α, p=β, p=γ.
'Π:z' notation: Π:0=0 as printed; 'ut sit Π:z=∫Zdz' is correct.
